analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; it sat on the Senate calendar until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent instead of letting them expire at the end of 2012, and would permanently raise the exemption for the alternative minimum tax. Its largest single provision would repeal the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax entirely, and it would cut the top gift tax rate to 35% with a $5 million lifetime exemption. Only seven Republican senators sponsored it, no Democrat did, and the Senate never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: All income-tax payers would keep the lower rate schedules from 2001 and 2003, and middle-income families benefit from the permanent alternative minimum tax patch and the retained child tax credit. But the largest dollar benefits go to households at the top: the permanent 15% rates on capital gains and dividends, the outright repeal of the estate and generation-skipping taxes, and the cheaper gift tax all flow overwhelmingly to the wealthiest families and their heirs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthiest households, large estates, and all taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Makes every provision of the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001 permanent, including the lower income-tax rate schedules and the child tax credit, by deleting the law's expiration date [S2][S3].
Makes permanent the reduced tax rates on capital gains and dividends enacted in 2003, which principally benefit households with investment income [S2][S3].

Permanently raises the alternative minimum tax exemption to $74,450 for married couples and $48,450 for singles and indexes both to inflation, sparing millions of households a tax originally aimed at the very top [S2][S3].
Repeals the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax entirely for deaths and transfers after enactment [S2][S3].
Cuts the maximum gift tax rate to 35% and allows a $5 million lifetime tax-free gift exemption, making it cheaper to pass wealth to heirs during life [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The bill includes no offsets, so the forgone revenue from lower rates, estate tax repeal, and the AMT patch would be made up through larger deficits and interest costs, or through future tax increases and spending cuts. Because the largest tax cuts go to high earners and large estates, the revenue loss is not proportional to the population's income.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate and generation-skipping taxes eliminates a tax that applied only to estates above the exemption amount, concentrating the entire revenue loss on the wealthiest few thousand estates each year while removing billions from federal revenue [S2][S3].

The bill makes the tax cuts permanent with no offsetting revenue, so it adds to federal deficits over time rather than being paid for, and the cost compounds as the AMT exemption and rates continue year after year [S2][S3].

A good-faith supporter's honest concession: the permanent low rates on capital gains and dividends are worth far more to the top few percent of households, who hold most investment income, than to a typical working family.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill genuinely protects middle-income families from the alternative minimum tax and from the across-the-board sunset of the 2001 and 2003 cuts, which would have raised many families' tax bills. But its design is heavily weighted toward the top: the estate tax repeal and the gift-tax changes benefit a small number of very wealthy families in dollar terms far out of proportion to their share of the population, and nothing in the bill pays for any of it. The cost is carried by everyone else through deficits or future tax increases.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late July 2012, read twice, and placed on the Senate's calendar of business, but the Senate never debated it or voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on July 23, 2012 with six Republican cosponsors: Sens. Rubio, Risch, DeMint, Cornyn, Vitter, and Johnson [S1][S3][S4].
It was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 472 on July 24, 2012 [S1][S5].
No further action was ever taken: no committee reported it, no debate occurred, and no vote was scheduled before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].
The bill arrived weeks before the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts were set to expire at the end of 2012; the eventual resolution came through separate end-of-year legislation, not this bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax survived, and the pressure to extend every 2001 and 2003 provision permanently was not advanced by this measure. The wealthiest households and large estates are worse off than they would have been under the bill, and federal revenue is higher than it would have been; the eventual tax compromise reached in separate legislation kept most cuts but not the full repeal this bill sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal revenue and the estate tax

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 23, 2012 and placed it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: Six Senate Republican cosponsors (Rubio, Risch, DeMint, Cornyn, Vitter, Johnson)

against.name: Sen. Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote; it remained on the calendar until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-led Senate never brought the bill to a vote.

industries.note: The bill would repeal the estate and generation-skipping taxes outright and cut the gift tax rate to 35% with a $5 million lifetime exemption, letting the largest fortunes pass to heirs untaxed. Their gain is the public's cost through lost federal revenue, with nothing in the bill to offset it [S2][S3].

Making the 2003 reduced rates on capital gains and dividends permanent primarily benefits the households and funds that hold most investment income, who are concentrated at the top of the income distribution. The permanent rate would be a guaranteed benefit compared with the scheduled sunset [S2][S3].

The permanent alternative minimum tax patch (with inflation indexing) and the retained child tax credit would keep tax bills lower for millions of ordinary families. This is the part of the bill where the interest of ordinary households runs alongside the bill's purpose, though it is the smaller share of the bill's total cost [S2][S3].
